title: Short-Sightedness (Myopia)
short_intro: Short-sightedness, or myopia, is a refractive defect of the eye in which parallel rays of light from a distant object are focused in front of the retina rather than directly on it. Consequently, distant objects appear blurred while near objects are seen clearly.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition, anatomical cause (elongation of eyeball or excessive curvature of cornea), identification of corrective lens (concave lens), and basic numericals involving far point and lens power.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed optical ray tracing, calculation of focal length and power for a given far point, accommodation range alterations, and combination of lenses for complete correction.

prerequisites: Lens Maker's Formula and thin lens equation
Anatomy and working of the human eye

concept_notes.heading: Anatomical and Optical Causes of Myopia
bullets: The eyeball gets elongated along its optical axis, increasing the distance between the eye lens and the retina.
The curvature of the cornea or the eye lens becomes too great, yielding excessive converging power.
Because of the high convergence, parallel rays from infinity form a real image in the vitreous humor before reaching the retina.

concept_notes.heading: Far Point of a Myopic Eye
bullets: For a normal human eye, the far point is at infinity (u = -\infty).
For a myopic eye, the far point (x) is at a finite distance in front of the eye.
Rays coming from any point beyond this finite far point cannot be focused on the retina without optical correction.

concept_notes.heading: Correction Using a Concave Lens
bullets: A diverging (concave) lens is used to correct myopia.
The concave lens intercepts parallel rays from infinity and diverges them such that they appear to come from the patient's actual far point.
The virtual image of a distant object formed by the corrective lens lies at the far point of the myopic eye, enabling the eye lens to focus it sharply on the retina.

concept_notes.heading: Optical Power and Focal Length Sign Convention
bullets: The focal length of the correcting concave lens must be negative.
The magnitude of the focal length of the corrective lens is precisely equal to the distance of the myopic far point from the eye.
The power of the corrective lens is negative, expressed in diopters (D).

derivations.title: Derivation of Focal Length of Corrective Concave Lens
derivations.conditions: Object at infinity (u = -\infty) must form a virtual image at the eye's far point (v = -x).
steps: Substitute the object distance for a distant object requiring correction: u = -\infty
Substitute the required image position at the patient's far point: v = -x

derivations.title: Derivation of Lens Power for Finite Object Distance
derivations.conditions: Object at a new distance u (where |u| > x) mapped to the far point v = -x.
steps: Substitute v = -x and the specific object distance u
Calculate the required focal length: f = \frac{xu}{x - u}
Express lens power P as P = \frac{1}{f(\text{in meters})}

graphs_and_experiments.title: Myopic Eye Ray Diagram
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Parallel rays entering an elongated eyeball and converging to a focal point in front of the retina.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates the anatomical defect where distant objects form blurred images before reaching the retina.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in TGT/PGT subjective and diagram-based identification questions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Correction of Myopia Using Concave Lens
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Parallel rays diverging through a concave lens before entering the myopic eye, forming a virtual image at the far point and final sharp image on the retina.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates how a diverging lens adjusts the incoming wavefront vergence to match the eye's reduced accommodation range.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in multi-part numerical and conceptual optical design questions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Power vs. Far Point Distance Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A hyperbola plot of Lens Power P (in D) on the y-axis versus Far Point x (in meters) on the x-axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that as the far point moves closer to the eye (severe myopia), the required corrective power increases non-linearly in magnitude.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Interpreting graphical trends in advanced PGT screening questions.

solved_numericals.question: A myopic person cannot see objects distinctly beyond 80 cm from the eye. What is the nature and power of the lens required to enable him to see distant objects clearly?
solution_steps: Identify the far point: x = 80 cm = 0.8 m.
Determine the nature of the lens: Since it is myopia, a concave (diverging) lens is required.

solved_numericals.question: A myopic physicist has a far point of 50 cm. She wishes to read a book placed at 25 cm without glasses, but her near point has also shifted. However, focusing strictly on her myopia correction for viewing an object at 150 cm, what power lens is required?
solution_steps: Far point x = 50 cm = 0.5 m. Desired object distance u = -150 cm = -1.5 m.
Apply lens formula: 1 / f = (1 / v) - (1 / u).
Set image distance v to the far point: v = -50 cm = -0.5 m.
Calculate power P = 1 / f = -4 / 3 D = -1.33 D.

solved_numericals.question: The far point of a myopic eye is 1.5 m. Find the focal length of the lens used to see the stars clearly.
solution_steps: For viewing stars (infinity), object distance u = -\infty.
Using f = -x, the required focal length is f = -1.5 m.

assumptions_and_limitations: The eye is modeled as a single refracting surface or a simplified thin lens system.
Astigmatism or other concurrent higher-order aberrations of the cornea are neglected.
The distance between the corrective spectacle lens and the eye lens (vertex distance) is assumed negligible in basic formulas unless specified.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A myopic person has difficulty seeing near objects.
common_misconceptions.correct: A myopic person can see near objects clearly; they have difficulty seeing distant objects.
common_misconceptions.why: The near point of a myopic eye is often closer than normal, but the far point is restricted to a finite distance.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A convex lens is used to correct short-sightedness.
common_misconceptions.correct: A concave lens is used to correct short-sightedness.
common_misconceptions.why: Short-sightedness requires diverging the incoming light rays to shift the image back onto the retina, which is the function of a concave lens.

quick_revision: Myopia = Short-sightedness = Image formed in front of retina = Corrected by Concave lens = Negative power.
Corrective Focal Length for Far Point x: f = -x
